#5520. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5519. This Violinist Beat 350,000 Applicants to Become Snoop Dogg’s $10,000-a-Month Ice Cream Taster — Here’s How She Struck a Chord

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Concert violinist Annabelle Traves explains how she scored a $10,000-a-month gig tasting ice cream for Snoop Dogg’s company

How did Annabelle Traves land the sweetest job on the planet? Let’s just say she pulled some strings.

The concert violinist, who has soloed at Carnegie Hall and the Sydney Opera House, was just named Dr. Bombay’s first International Ice Cream Taster. In August, Snoop Dogg’s ice cream brand put out a call for the job, which pays $10,000 a month. More than 350,000 people from 130+ countries applied through HR and payroll platform Deel, which ran the search.

Traves, an Australian based in Dubai, starts a three-month contract helping Dr. Bombay expand into new markets, dream up new flavors and create a Deel-themed ice cream. Entrepreneur caught up with Traves to talk about her latest gig.

What did you submit to beat out all those other applicants?I decided to play to my strengths. Many of the other applicants owned dairy farms or had spent years researching dairy. I love ice cream, but I wouldn’t call myself a dairy expert, so I leaned on what I knew best. In my application video, I plucked a little of one of Snoop’s famous melodies on my violin. When I made the top 15, I doubled down with my own cover of “Young, Wild & Free.” I think that musical connection is part of what caught Snoop’s attention.

You’re already a very successful violinist. Why go after a gig like this?The timing was perfect. I had just come off a world tour with André Rieu, and for the first time in years I didn’t have a schedule that I had to coordinate a year in advance. Then there was the ice cream, and who doesn’t love ice cream? And of course, Snoop himself. I love all genres of music and have always loved his, so the chance to bond with him as a fellow musician was hugely appealing.

What do you look for when you’re tasting a new flavor?In one word, novelty. I want a flavor I’ve never tried before. Vanilla has been done a billion times. Dr. Maya, who develops the flavors at Dr. Bombay, introduced me to the idea that ice cream flavors develop over time. A couple of seconds in, a different flavor comes through. People talk about that with wine, but I’d never experienced such sophisticated flavors in ice cream until I tried Dr. Bombay. The nostalgia of the brand also stands out. Flavors like Sherbet take you right back as a 90s kid, and Peanut Butter Jelly Time does the same. I’d love to find flavors based on popular candies or afternoon snacks from those days.

#5518. Big Tech’s AI race will save small business owners time. It won’t find them customers

Eric Groves is the CEO and co-founder of Alignable, a networking platform for small business owners, and was a founding executive at Constant Contact. Alignable’s AI assistant, Allie, is named in this piece.

Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic are racing to become the small business owner’s AI assistant. Meta brought its Muse agent to small businesses in September. Anthropic and OpenAI now package tools aimed squarely at owners, and Google is building the same features into tools millions of them already use.

That competition is good for Main Street. But it’s a race to save owners time, and time isn’t what keeps them up at night. What keeps them up is where the next customer will come from.

A word on where I sit. I run Alignable, a network of 10 million small business owners, so I have a stake in this argument. Alignable also co-hosts small business AI training with Anthropic, one of the companies named here. Read what follows with that in mind. But I also have something the assistants don’t: 13 years of data on how small businesses actually find work.

Start with where customers come from. In our surveys, members say about 85% of their customers come through referrals. Not ads, not search, not cold email. People who already trust them.

Across 35,000 local communities, our members have formed 226 million business connections. Most of them never become a relationship that sends work either way. The owners who grow through their networks aren’t the ones with the most connections. I’ve told owners for years that 50 warm relationships beat 500 cold contacts. That’s a rule of thumb from experience, not a number we’ve measured. But the owners who win do keep a small set of relationships active and leave the rest alone.

And most owners are sitting on more opportunity than they know. When members tell us what their ideal customer looks like, we can count how many of those businesses sit one introduction away: connected to someone the owner already knows. Among members whose ideal customers show up in their extended network, the typical one has about 190 of them a single introduction away. For one in four, it’s more than 600.

The next customer is rarely a stranger. They’re one relationship away, through someone the owner hasn’t talked to in months.

Those relationships aren’t random, either. In my experience, three kinds do most of the work: customers who talk you up, businesses that serve the same customer without competing with you, and a handful of people who open doors. The best referral partner usually isn’t a peer in your own industry. It’s the business your customer calls right before or right after they call you: the realtor and the home inspector, the accountant and the financial planner.

Ask any of the big assistants how to get more referrals and you’ll get a solid list of best practices. Ask an assistant that sits on a map of business relationships and it can tell you something specific: three nearby businesses serve your ideal customer, one of them already knows two of your clients, and you haven’t spoken to your best referral partner in four months.

That’s the difference between advice and action. A general assistant can’t answer that question, because the answer lives in data it doesn’t have.

The early numbers bear this out. In Bluehost’s 2026 study of 350 U.S. owners, 78% said AI saves them time every week. But 43% have seen no change in revenue. Time saved only matters if it goes somewhere that pays.

Too often it goes into volume. Forbes recently told the story of Paul Birrell, a New Jersey owner whose automation loop sent roughly 400,000 emails in three days. His reaction: “I don’t have 400,000 customers.” Everything we see says growth comes from the opposite: judgment about the few people who matter.

AI will reach small business owners in three forms. The first is the personal assistant the giants are fighting over. It delivers time, and the assistants are converging fast.

The second is AI built into the systems that already hold the business’s own data. Intuit knows the books. Shopify knows the store. That AI delivers control: it can flag a cash crunch six weeks out or spot the product quietly losing money.

The third is AI built on the relationships between businesses: who knows whom, who serves the same customers, who sends work to whom. That’s the one that delivers growth, and it’s the one almost nobody is talking about. At Alignable, ours is called Allie.

The giants have real advantages, and they’ll connect to the other two kinds. Meta’s Muse already plugs into QuickBooks, Shopify and Stripe, and the others are adding similar connections. The open question is who the intelligence works for. Meta makes nearly all of its money selling ads, and an assistant built by an ad company will tend to find that the answer involves more advertising. The data that actually works for the owner describes how their business runs and who in their community can help it grow.

Use a personal assistant every day. The time savings are real.

Then decide, in advance, where the reclaimed hours go. Put them on the calendar against the work that generates revenue, and the most neglected item on that list is relationships. Write down the 50 people most likely to send you business. Most owners can name 10 without trying. Those 10 are where AI should be pointing you.

There are about 36 million small businesses in the U.S., and more than 80% of them have no employees. For those owners, AI isn’t a department upgrade. It’s a capability they never had. Owners should take the better tools the giants’ race produces. But the biggest gains won’t come from saving an hour. They’ll come from knowing which 50 relationships to spend it on.

#5517. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5516. How I Built a Fully Remote Global Team Without Spending a Dollar on Job Ads or Recruiters

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Solopreneurs that provide digital services have a world of talent at their disposal. Here is how to leverage it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Solopreneurship, despite its name, is anything but a solo pursuit. As we find success in our agency work, we inevitably need to build a team that can help us serve our clients and expand our footprint.

As MVRK, my CRM strategy and implementation consulting agency, starts its seventh fiscal year, I’m very happy to say that my team is now composed of seven individuals who operate from six different countries. What’s more, none of us live in the three countries where we mainly do business (USA, Canada and the UK).

I have hired each of the individuals who are on the team myself. And I discovered them in a unique but repeatable way. In this article, I’m going to review the method that I’ve used to build those relationships with potential talent and share how I’ve been able to make them a part of my team. All with zero dollars spent.

For the first three years of running my business, I operated fully solo. But as I started to build success, I had an important realization: The clients that enjoyed working with me did not want to leave.

One of the projects that I worked on in my early years was implementing an entire Salesforce CRM system from the ground up for a Philippines-based recruitment agency. This agency was staffing talent in North America, so I knew I had a connection I could leverage to find that initial team member.

I defined the requirements, and that recruitment agency put some talent in front of me. From there, I selected somebody who I felt was going to work. I believe that I got quite lucky with my first hire because that individual is still a member of my team.

While I support the recruitment agency model and believe it works for many companies, the reality is that an agency is still a middleman that does not add a tremendous amount of value.  In my case, eventually, the individual in question wanted to continue working with me, without having to go through the agency. As a result, we formed a relationship directly.

Of course, it’s important to check any terms of service that you’ve signed before you make this kind of transition. But using an agency is not the only option. There is a way that you can leverage remote talent without relying on the offshore recruiting industry. It’s a little bit more work, but it’s a lot more rewarding for both you and the talent that you hire.

As we come to the end of 2026 and move towards 2027, you need to realize that relying on talent only in your immediate geographic area is limiting your ability to grow. Except for industries where in-person presence is required for regulatory or delivery purposes, there is no reason why you should limit yourself to hiring people in your city, in your state or province, or in your country.

This world is big, and there’s talent to be found in a lot more places than just your backyard. The best way that I have found to discover that talent is to go to the online communities where they hang out, share their knowledge and build a network. Crucially, these are also the places where they can discover you without tremendous costs.

I have found Reddit in particular is an incredible source of talent. What’s more, I haven’t spent a single dollar on advertising job ads or on recruiter fees. I’ve been able to build those relationships myself. Reddit has various communities, many that are specifically niched to your industry, and it is those places where individuals from across the world are hanging out.

To find talent via Reddit communities, I’ve built simple intake forms asking the right questions to vet individuals. Forget about asking for resumes. Instead, my process is simple. I share a request for talent in a relevant community, ensuring I follow the rules of that community. Within that request, I ask people to fill in my form as a first step. This gives me everything I need to find individuals who look like the best potential options and invite them for an interview.

From here, I vet them using the standard process and offer extended initial term contracts to those who are a good fit. Extended initial term contracts are ideal in this situation. They allow you to extend the term if you find you work together effectively, but also provide a clean separation if things don’t work out.

As you can see, there’s no need to pay somebody else to find talent for you. For many solopreneurs, this is a waste of money and time. Instead, go to relevant online communities (Reddit is just one option) where those individuals hang out, build real relationships with them and hire the right people for your team. It’s a valuable route to solopreneur success.

Solopreneurship, despite its name, is anything but a solo pursuit. As we find success in our agency work, we inevitably need to build a team that can help us serve our clients and expand our footprint.

In this article, I’m going to review the method that I’ve used to build those relationships with potential talent and share how I’ve been able to make them a part of my team. All with zero dollars spent.

#5515. The battle for megawatts: why restricting data centers is a strategic mistake

Serhiy Tokarev is co-founder and general partner at Roosh, a Ukrainian investment group whose portfolio includes AI infrastructure and energy companies.

In Ireland, data centers consume nearly a quarter of the country’s electricity. New grid connections around Dublin were effectively frozen for three years. Under revised rules, new projects must provide generation or storage capacity onsite or nearby. Amsterdam previously imposed a moratorium on new facilities, while Frankfurt regulates their location through zoning.

In July 2026, New York State introduced a moratorium of up to one year on certain environmental permits for new large data centers. State officials said the pause would allow them to assess the facilities’ impact on the power grid and the environment. As of May 2026, data center projects representing nearly 12 GW of potential demand were in the state’s grid interconnection queue.

Should governments restrict data centers when power grids cannot keep pace? I believe they should expand power supply and grid capacity instead.

As co-founder and general partner of Roosh Investment Group, I have been investing in technology companies for over five years. Our portfolio includes AI infrastructure, and energy is now a key focus. This experience has shown me how access to energy infrastructure influences investment decisions. Reliable power is increasingly becoming a decisive factor in a company’s ability to scale and attract capital.

As businesses rely more on AI, control over its models and infrastructure matters more. A foreign provider’s decision to change terms, raise prices, or restrict access could affect entire industries. Domestic computing capacity gives countries more control over the infrastructure their businesses depend on.

This helps explain the intensity of U.S.–China competition in AI. American companies hold leading positions across the AI stack, from advanced models and chips to major cloud platforms. Washington views the power supply for data center infrastructure as a national security issue.

Beijing is pursuing a state-led strategy. Its “Eastern Data, Western Computing” program directs the development of computing capacity toward western China, where energy and land resources are more readily available. At the same time, the country is expanding power generation at scale. According to the International Energy Agency, China added nearly 500 GW of renewable capacity in 2025—more than 60% of the global increase.

Europe, meanwhile, risks falling further behind. Brussels plans up to seven AI gigafactories and at least a tripling of EU data center capacity within five to seven years. Yet some countries are slowing construction, while European businesses still rely primarily on American cloud providers. Restrictions do not remove demand for AI; they risk pushing investment abroad and reinforcing that dependence.

Data centers’ hunger for power should be understood in the context of wider electricity demand. According to the International Energy Agency, they accounted for only around 70 TWh of the 800 TWh increase in global electricity consumption in 2025. Industry, air conditioning, heat pumps, and electric vehicles contributed far more.

The challenge is rapidly growing demand concentrated in a handful of locations. Power must reach new computing capacity in time.

In the U.S., lead times for large transformers now exceed two years, compared with roughly 50 weeks before the pandemic. Morgan Stanley estimates that U.S. data centers could face a power shortfall of around 49 GW by 2028. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has acknowledged that power has become the company’s binding constraint. Some of its GPUs are sitting in inventory with nowhere to plug them in.

Dedicated gas-fired plants offer no quick fix. GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, and Mitsubishi Power produce around two-thirds of the world’s gas turbines, and their factories are booked years ahead. GE Vernova reported 116 GW in gas power equipment orders and slot reservations, while targeting annual turbine output of 20 GW in the third quarter of 2026.

The hardware itself adds another challenge. A server rack once required 7–12 kW. Systems built around NVIDIA’s GB200 consume 120–132 kW per rack. Conventional air cooling is no longer sufficient at that power density, so new facilities must be designed for liquid cooling from the outset.

Tech giants are securing power themselves. Microsoft agreed to buy electricity from the 835 MW Three Mile Island reactor, which is being restarted to serve its needs. Google’s agreement with Kairos Power calls for small modular reactors, with the first expected online by 2030.

Governments cannot rely on corporate initiative alone. They must plan energy and digital infrastructure together: expand grids, accelerate transformer production, streamline connections, and encourage long-term power purchase agreements, generation near data centers, and storage.

Ukraine’s experience shows how a crisis can accelerate the deployment of local generation. War and repeated attacks forced the country to rapidly deploy local power sources where the centralized grid could no longer guarantee a reliable supply.

My experience investing in technology companies has shown me that reliable infrastructure is essential for business growth. In Ukraine, companies have long had to manage energy risks. They need reliable electricity, backup power, and plans for potential outages. This also matters to investors. A company’s ability to operate during power outages affects how they assess its potential for growth.

Ukraine already has around 1.8 GW of distributed gas-fired generation, with more than 500 MW under construction. It is also streamlining grid connection and permitting procedures.

Ukraine’s experience cannot be directly applied to large AI data centers. But it illustrates how making energy resilience a priority can accelerate investment in additional generation and changes to connection procedures, even under extreme conditions.

Powering new data centers will require coordinated action by governments, grid operators, and businesses. Governments can plan sites for new facilities. Grid operators can reserve capacity for them in advance. Businesses can invest in their own power plants, storage, and cooling, and reduce electricity use during peak hours in exchange for faster grid connections. A combination of grid supply, gas-fired plants, nuclear power, and renewables can help meet demand where no single source is sufficient.

The ability to build and power data centers quickly is likely to become an increasingly important factor in investment decisions. An advantage in the AI race will depend not only on access to models and chips, but also on a country’s ability to expand computing capacity, generation, and grids together. Restricting data center development may temporarily ease grid pressure, but it can also deepen dependence on foreign infrastructure and technology.

#5514. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5513. Your Business May Be Invisible to AI. Here Are 7 Simple Fixes You Can Make This Week.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Learn how to improve AI visibility with seven practical website, content and credibility fixes that help customers discover and evaluate your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

Start with customer language, not marketing jargon. If you sell cybersecurity services to banks, someone may ask, “Who helps regional banks prepare for a security audit?” They are less likely to type your carefully crafted positioning statement. Your first job is to understand the questions that occur before a buying decision.

Write five to 10 realistic prompts from sales calls, customer emails and proposal requests. Include a category question, a problem question, a comparison question and one that names your market. Test them in more than one AI search experience. Record the date, precise wording, companies mentioned, cited sources and whether your own website is among those sources.

Keep branded prompts separate. “Tell me about Acme Consulting” checks brand recognition; “Which firms can improve manufacturing supply-chain forecasting?” investigates discovery by an unfamiliar buyer. Confusing the two creates false confidence.

Your 20-minute action: Create a spreadsheet with columns for prompt, platform, date, cited source, competitor and opportunity. Treat observations as directional research, not an audited visibility score. Repeat the same prompt set monthly to look for persistent patterns.

Too many homepages use language that could describe any company: “We unlock transformational growth through next-generation solutions.” It sounds sophisticated but leaves a buyer wondering what is actually for sale. If a customer cannot understand the offer in ten seconds, that is a messaging problem long before it becomes a technical SEO problem.

Replace abstraction with a simple structure: “We help [specific audience] solve [specific problem] through [specific product or service], so they can [realistic outcome].” For example: “We help multi-location clinics improve patient acquisition and appointment conversion through search, content and website optimization.”

Then add proof nearby: industries served, a concrete capability, a customer example or a documented credential. Do not paste an entire keyword list into your opening paragraph. Make the first 100 words accurate, readable and specific, with one primary H1 that matches the subject of the page.

Your 20-minute action: Ask someone outside your organization to read the first screen of your homepage. Can they explain whom you serve, what you deliver and what action to take next? If not, rewrite it before investing in additional content.

Businesses often publish broad thought leadership but hide the details a buyer needs: price ranges, implementation steps, eligibility, limitations and alternatives. That leaves both customers and answer-generating systems with incomplete information.

Ask sales and customer-service teams which questions recur immediately before someone books a meeting or requests a quote. Select five. Build accurate answers into the relevant service or product pages, not a disconnected wall of generic FAQs. Use a descriptive H2 question and answer it directly in the first sentence, followed by examples, constraints and the next decision a buyer needs to make.

If pricing varies, explain the variables rather than inventing a price. If delivery timelines depend on approvals, say so. If the product is not suitable for every customer, acknowledge that explicitly. Useful answers increase confidence because they reduce uncertainty, not because they repeat a search phrase.

This approach aligns with a broader shift toward commercially useful content. For additional perspective, Entrepreneur has covered how businesses can earn leads across both AI search and conventional Google discovery.

Your 45-minute action: Publish one complete answer on each of your top five revenue-driving pages. Review the result on mobile. Does a buyer get the information without opening an accordion, guessing terminology or scheduling a sales call?

“Trusted,” “innovative” and “industry-leading” are not proof. Any competitor can make the same claims. Instead, help a skeptical prospect verify what you say. That might mean a named subject-matter expert, clear methodology, customer references with consent, original observations, dated research, documented product features or a candid case study.

An effective case study explains the initial problem, what changed, how success was measured and what the outcome means. A claimed 300% improvement without a baseline is less persuasive than a transparent account of the metric, time period and relevant limitations. Not every business can disclose client names, but permissioned or anonymized evidence can still be useful if presented accurately.

For expertise-led services, include author credentials, an updated bio and an explanation of who is responsible for the advice. For regulated industries, prioritize accurate, appropriately reviewed content over speed.

Your 30-minute action: Select your most profitable service page and add one piece of verifiable evidence plus a short explanation of why it matters to the buyer. Then identify what proof is still missing.

You can write a perfect page and undermine it with a noindex directive, a broken canonical tag, restrictive robots rules or weak internal linking. Start by checking the pages that generate or could generate revenue. Avoid treating technical optimization as a giant sitewide project when a focused inspection of five pages will reveal practical priorities.

Use Google Search Console to inspect indexing and important search queries. Confirm that key page content is present as readable text, accessible from relevant navigation and consistent with its title and meta description. Structured data can support eligible search features when it accurately represents visible content, but no special schema guarantees inclusion in AI answers.

Google’s official guidance for generative AI search reinforces that strong SEO foundations and distinctive, useful content remain central. There is no requirement to purchase a special AI markup package.

If you want public pages eligible for inclusion in ChatGPT Search, examine bot-access policies too. OpenAI distinguishes its search crawler from other crawlers, so site owners should review the current documentation rather than assuming all AI bot traffic serves the same purpose.

Your 30-minute action: Inspect five commercially important URLs for index eligibility, broken links, visible text and relevant internal links. Assign each issue to a named owner with a completion date.

A website is necessary, but it is also a controlled channel. Buyers often validate a company through independent sources, including industry associations, credible media, customer reviews, professional directories and expert participation. Those sources are valuable because they can corroborate facts, not because a business purchased a large volume of mentions.

Start with accuracy: Is your business name consistent? Are leaders and services described correctly? Are your credentials up to date? Can a customer find substantive contributions rather than a directory entry alone? Then focus on places that matter in your market. A healthcare founder may benefit more from a recognized professional association or reputable sector publication than a generic syndication network.

Entrepreneur has also examined the role of credible outside recognition in a changing search environment. The practical lesson is to earn citations and mentions through work worth referencing rather than mechanically distributing the same press release everywhere.

Your 45-minute action: Correct three important third-party profiles, then identify one legitimate opportunity to contribute an original data point, expert explanation or customer insight to an industry publication.

It is tempting to turn AI visibility into a single number. But being named frequently does not guarantee revenue, and AI answers are inconsistent enough that screenshots are a weak stand-alone measurement system. Separate the signals you can observe from the outcomes your organization actually needs.

Track whether your brand appears for a consistent set of buyer questions. Record citations where platforms expose them. Review identifiable AI referral traffic in analytics, but recognize that some journeys will not carry an obvious referral label. Combine those indicators with form submissions, qualified meetings, pipeline and revenue. Ask new prospects how they discovered you, while understanding that self-reported attribution is imperfect.

For leadership reporting, a simple monthly scorecard beats a glossy dashboard that cannot explain its methodology. Show changes to priority pages, visible search and referral trends, sales opportunities and what you plan to test next. Make it clear which trends are observed, estimated or unavailable.

Your 30-minute action: Establish a baseline this month and choose one commercial metric to improve. A rise in citations may be encouraging; a rise in qualified opportunities is the outcome the business can use.

Do not confuse a seven-day implementation sprint with seven-day rankings. Search systems can take time to discover and process changes. Results depend on competition, platform behavior, website quality and the strength of your evidence. The point of the sprint is to eliminate obvious weaknesses and create a defensible plan.

AI search has changed the way some buyers research providers, but it has not removed the need for fundamentals. A clear offer, useful answers, accessible pages, credible evidence and disciplined measurement improve the experience for the human buyer first. They also give discovery systems more accurate material to work with.

The question for business owners is not, “How do I trick AI into recommending me?” It is, “Have I given customers and credible sources enough useful information to understand why my company belongs on the shortlist?” That is a much more productive place to begin.

For organizations that want to examine these issues more systematically, I use an AI visibility assessment approach through Bullzeye Media Marketing’s GEO practice. The same starting principle applies whether you work with an advisor or manage it internally: Diagnose the gaps before spending on execution.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

#5512. This CEO lived on canned soup and took just two days off for his daughter’s birth. Now, he admits he lost sight of proper work-life balance

The grind to success can be long, punishing, and it can quietly take more than it gives.

Ron Schneidermann knows that better than most.

After scaling his first company, Liftopia, into a business with more than $60 million in annual revenue, he went on to become CEO of AllTrails, the popular hiking map app. Today, he leads test-prep startup Acely. But looking back across his career, he says he had to learn the hard way what real work-life balance actually costs—and what it’s worth.

While building Liftopia, a digital marketplace for ski resorts, that mindset came at a personal price. Schneidermann worked out of a cramped San Francisco apartment, turned spending less than $15 a day into a kind of endurance test, and went two years without taking a salary, surviving largely on canned soup.

The tradeoffs even extended into his family life. When his first daughter was born four years into Liftopia, he took just two days off work. Three years later, he allowed himself just a week for his son’s birth—and thought that was progress.

“I look back, I was just able to justify it as ‘that’s just part of the grind’… but you never get that time back,” Schneidermann told Fortune. “That was a mistake.”

It’s not an easy admission in startup culture, where sacrifice is often worn as a badge of honor and overwork is normalized as the price of ambition. But Schneidermann, now in his late 40s, has since reframed the experience entirely.

“For everything that was frustrating, that went wrong, that I regretted about Liftopia, I was able to take the inverse and turn it into a strength,” he said.

By the time he joined AllTrails in 2015, that mindset shift was already underway. He eventually became CEO in 2019 and instituted a company-wide ritual: the first Friday of every month, AllTrails shut down and employees were encouraged to go outside.

In August 2025, he took on the new challenge of becoming CEO of Acely. This time, he’s bringing those hard-won lessons with him from the start. Instead of monthly trail days, the company now runs a monthly “hackathon,” where its less than a dozen employees pause routine work for the whole day and experiment with AI tools and new ideas—no meetings, no KPIs, no deliverables.

Even before Schneidermann had his eyes on entrepreneurship, he was learning career lessons the hard way.

In the late 1990s, he was a student at UCLA studying mass communication and business while also working at Abercrombie & Fitch to help pay for his studies. However, he ended up getting fired three separate times because he “never liked it” enough to muster the proper decorum.

Similarly, after graduating in 2000, he landed a job at Accenture working as a business process consultant. Once again, though, he found it not aligning with the life he wanted to have. And despite the lucrative salary of working at a Fortune 500 consulting firm, he quit.

“It was a great experience. I’m grateful for it, but I hated it,” he said. “I hated it, and I told myself, I am never going to take a job for money again. Life is too short.”

That realization eventually pushed him toward startups.

Through a friend of a friend, he landed a role at Hotwire, then a travel startup that was later acquired by Expedia, and it became his entry point into the tech world. Looking back, Schneidermann said that early career path offers a lesson he wishes more young workers would take seriously: relationships matter as much as résumés, especially in a job market where traditional entry-level pipelines are narrowing.

“Really invest in your network,” he said. “There’s a small pond at the end of the day. If you stay in it long enough, you are going to know everyone, and everyone you know are going to be leaders somewhere.”

Schneidermann’s point may resonate with Gen Z at a time when employers say early-career workers are struggling with basic professional norms. A 2024 survey found that six in 10 bosses admitted they had already fired Gen Z employees hired straight out of college, citing poor communication, lack of professionalism, and disorganization.

For Schneidermann, the issue isn’t just skills—it’s mindset. Too many young workers treat networking as transactional, when in reality it’s built on consistency, reputation, and how you show up over time. That starts with small, often overlooked behaviors.

“There’s a human on the other end. Don’t ghost people and just show up,” he said.

The same principle applies more broadly to career growth. Rather than chasing the perfect role or obsessing over credentials, Schneidermann emphasized curiosity as the real differentiator.

“Just approach everything with a curious mindset,” he added. “Just constantly try to be learning and exploring.”

That philosophy has carried through multiple career pivots, including his most recent move to Acely, a startup with no obvious connection to his background. After being approached by an executive search firm, he took the job in part because his high school–aged daughter had recently used the product for SAT prep. She was among its over 50,000 active users.

For Schneidermann, the challenge was one he was eager to take on. From his perspective, he didn’t need to be an expert in the industry—he just needed to be willing to learn it.

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5510. Tight Budget? This Familiar Destination Could Help You Cut Expenses.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With less room in their budgets, people are turning to a familiar resource they may have overlooked.

Shoppers looking to cut costs are rediscovering an old favorite location in their neighborhoods: their local library.

According to a new report from NPR, consumers are returning to the library to get more without stretching their paychecks.

One avid reader, Izzy Rivera, picks up at least one book a week from local libraries near her residence in Topeka, Kansas. She said in an interview with NPR that it “just isn’t realistic” for her to regularly buy new books as she saves up for law school.

Rivera checks out both physical books and digital ones through the Libby library app. She isn’t ruling out buying books altogether. Last month, she went to her local library’s used book sale and bought 15 books for around $20.

There are other instances where the library provided Rivera with free or low-cost materials. For example, she watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, which requires a library card or university login.

Her library card also provides her with free access to The New York Times online, a perk that extends beyond her neighborhood. For example, The New York Public Library began offering visitors free access to The New York Times in January if they accessed the digital newspaper while on the library’s Wi-Fi network.

Rivera said she spends a lot of time at her local library.

“It’s somewhere I can go where I’m not expected to spend money,” she said. “If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn’t want a coffee.”

Librarians and library-goers across the country told NPR that financial pressures are drawing consumers into libraries. The pattern is familiar to library staff: When money gets tight, demand for their services grows.

Americans are cutting spending on optional items as they try to afford the necessities. A Pew Research Center report released last month found that 44% of Americans struggled to afford at least one basic necessity, like medical care or housing, over the previous year.

Meanwhile, 70% said they had trimmed spending on nonessentials like dining out and streaming subscriptions across the same time period. Pew Research conducted the survey in late August, and about 5,000 Americans responded.

Several of the nation’s largest public library systems showed NPR data reflecting recent increases in membership. More library-goers are also borrowing materials and attending events.

Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association, said in an interview with NPR that she attributes some of that growth to “heightened awareness” of what libraries offer.

Libraries “are especially popular right now, I think, because people are aware that everything that we provide is free or very low cost,” McCauley said.

#5509. Starter homes cost $1 million in a record 242 U.S. cities—proof the affordability crisis has hit the homes meant for first-time buyers

They waited out the pandemic boom. They saved longer, rented longer, delayed longer, and watched the typical first-time homebuyer age climb to a record 40. Now, the buyers who did everything right are running into a new problem: The Northeast just became the fastest-growing region for million-dollar starter homes in the country.

It’s especially imperfectly timed for millennials entering their peak household spending years and beginning to form their own families (or at least try to).

A Zillow report published in June counts a record 242 U.S. cities where starter homes cost $1 million or more—triple the 80 cities that cleared that mark before the pandemic, and up from 226 a year ago.

The share of first-time buyers has fallen to half the historical norm. For millennial parents in the Northeast—now in their late thirties and early forties, often with kids, hunting for more space—the numbers have a specific shape.

New Jersey had just one million-dollar starter city before the pandemic. Now it has 26. New York used to have 12; now it has 41. The two states added 15 cities to the list in the past year alone—faster growth than anywhere else in the country. The New York City metro area now leads all with 63 cities where a starter home runs $1 million or more.

That growth didn’t happen in a vacuum. Six of the 10 most competitive housing markets in the country are in the Northeast, per Zillow’s 2026 analysis, a region where new construction has chronically lagged and inventory deficits run deepest. California still leads the raw count with 105 cities, but the Northeast is where the crisis is actively spreading.

“A housing shortage a decade in the making ran headlong into intense demand with mortgage rates at historic lows, driving up home values at a record pace,” Zillow senior economist Kara Ng wrote. For Northeast buyers, those forces have compounded.

First-time homebuyers are historically younger, although the typical age of first-time buyers climbed to an all-time high of 40, according to a National Association of Realtors report released in November 2025. In fact, the housing market has gotten so unaffordable that the number of first-time homebuyers fell to half the historical norm last July.

A rising price floor on starter homes only pushes that first home purchase further out of reach. And it’s a problem that’s worsened, especially during the past couple of years.

“For homebuyers, the prevalence of million-dollar cities significantly—greatly—strains what is already the worst housing affordability since at least the 1980s,” Christopher M. Naghibi, executive vice president and chief operating officer at First Foundation Bank, told Fortune in 2024 when Zillow released a report about the number of U.S. cities with $1 million median-priced homes. “Prospective buyers in these markets face higher barriers to entry, needing ridiculously large down payments and higher incomes to afford homes.” That still holds true today.

Zillow defines a starter home as one in the lowest third of home values in a given region. As of June, the typical starter home nationwide was worth $198,649, up 1.7% from a year earlier. But in well over 200 U.S. cities, starter home prices are a whopping five times as high as that. It’s a phenomenon that keeps spreading, and into places it never used to touch.

Zillow chalks it up to the effects of the pandemic housing boom.

Before 2020, the list of cities with $1 million starter homes was almost all coastal. Colorado was the only non-coastal state with a million-dollar starter-home city. Now 26 states have at least one, up from nine before the pandemic. Texas, Wyoming, and Illinois each have multiple examples.

California still leads with 105 cities, but the fastest growth is in the Northeast. New York and New Jersey added 15 cities combined over the past year. New York is now up to 41, from just 12 before the pandemic. New Jersey is at 26, up from one.

The New York City metro area tops all metros with 63 cities where a starter home runs $1 million or more. San Francisco follows with 37, then Los Angeles with 33, San Jose with 13, and Miami and Seattle with eight each. The trend aligns with Zillow’s 2026 hottest markets analysis, which found six of the 10 most competitive housing markets are in the Northeast, where new construction has lagged and inventory deficits run deep.

The pandemic reset the cost of buying a home. A housing shortage a decade in the making collided with surging demand and historically low mortgage rates, pushing values up at a record pace. Those effects have stuck.

The squeeze on millennials and Gen Z has been building for years. Baby boomers, sitting on paid-off homes or cheap pandemic-era mortgages, have edged younger buyers out of the market in record numbers. The cost has pushed some Americans to delay milestones like marriage and kids, and others to co-buy homes with friends or partners just to split the bill.

Others have done the opposite—had kids first, rented longer, and are now hunting for space in a market that moved against them.

“We’re seeing a reshaping of the housing ladder,” Alexandra Gupta, a real-estate broker with the Corcoran Group, previously told Fortune. “Some first-time buyers are turning to long-term renting or even co-living models because the idea of owning a home has become so out of reach.”

There are modest signs of relief. Conditions are slowly turning friendlier for buyers. Zillow found the typical buyer now breaks even versus renting after about six years, down from more than eight in late 2023. More inventory and slower price growth mean buyers who are financially prepared are in better shape than they had been.

But “financially prepared” is carrying a lot of weight in 242 cities where there are $1 million starter homes. For a young buyer there, the costs pile up fast: a bigger down payment, a higher monthly mortgage, and a steeper climb before they achieve the American Dream.

No wonder that dream is largely happening in Texas.

#5508. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5507. Your Customers Are Using AI Search. They’re Still Googling You, Too. Here’s What Your Marketing Strategy Might Be Missing.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

A new audience-overlap finding is a useful corrective to the idea that AI search is replacing Google. And it changes how businesses should think about discovery and measurement.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I keep hearing a version of the same question from business leaders: Is AI search taking customers away from Google?

A new Similarweb audience-overlap figure offers a useful answer, with an important limit. In September, 93.7% of ChatGPT.com’s visitors also visited Google.com. The overlap ran the other way, too: 14.1% of Google.com’s visitors also visited ChatGPT.com, according to Search Engine Watch’s report.

That is not proof that someone asked ChatGPT about a product, then searched for it on Google. The data counts people who visited both websites during the month. It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

Those limits matter. But they don’t make the finding irrelevant. They tell us not to mistake channel overlap for channel substitution.

For years, marketers have organized discovery into tidy channels: search, social, referrals, paid media. AI assistants make that division harder to defend. A person might ask an AI tool to compare options, search a brand name in Google, watch a creator review, then visit a company’s site directly. The journey may cross several systems before the business gets a measurable click.

The Similarweb figure doesn’t prove that sequence. It does show why we shouldn’t assume that a visitor counted in an AI audience is a new person who has never used Google. Treating those groups as separate pools can lead to double-counting, inflated reach estimates and bad budget decisions.

I saw a version of this mistake when search was still new to many companies. Some treated SEO as a separate experiment instead of infrastructure for demand that already existed. The risk now is the reverse: treating AI discovery as a replacement for the search habits customers still have.

The better question isn’t which platform wins. It’s whether your brand is present, clear and credible when a customer moves between them.

The overlap stat also exposes a measurement problem. A customer might encounter a brand in an AI answer and later search for it by name. That later visit could show up as Google organic traffic, even if the earlier discovery helped create the demand. Or the AI interaction might never produce a visit at all. The audience-overlap data can’t tell us which happened.

That is why last-click reporting is a poor referee for this shift. A referral source can tell you where a session came from. It usually can’t tell you which earlier interactions made the brand worth looking up.

Google has begun giving site owners a clearer view of one part of the picture. Its Search Console generative AI performance report shows impressions for pages appearing in Google’s AI search features, including AI Overviews and AI Mode. That is useful visibility data, not proof of incremental traffic or revenue, and it doesn’t cover ChatGPT or other AI platforms.

Businesses should keep the measures separate. Track traditional search clicks, branded searches, qualified leads and sales. Alongside them, monitor which pages appear in Google’s AI features and whether your brand is cited in a consistent set of relevant AI prompts. Add a simple question to lead forms or post-purchase surveys: “Where did you first hear about us?” None of those signals proves, on its own, that AI caused a sale. Together, they can reveal patterns that last-click reports miss.

The response isn’t to split the marketing budget evenly between Google and AI. It’s to stop planning as if every platform reaches a different customer.

Keep investing in the parts of search that help customers find and evaluate you. Make sure the pages that explain your products, pricing and value are current. Understand which questions bring qualified prospects to your site. Then extend the same discipline to AI discovery: Check whether answer engines describe your business accurately, cite useful sources and include you when customers compare options.

Most importantly, connect the teams and dashboards. If SEO reports a decline in clicks while AI visibility rises, don’t declare one channel the winner and the other the loser. Look at branded search, lead quality, direct visits and conversion trends. Ask customers what influenced them. Compare the pattern over time, not just across one month’s traffic report.

I don’t read the 93.7% figure as evidence that Google is safe or that AI search is harmless to existing traffic. It doesn’t answer either question. I read it as a reason to be more precise: Customers can add a new way to discover a business without abandoning the old one.

Your customers may meet you in an AI answer and Google you before they act. The companies that understand both moments will make better decisions than the ones still asking which channel gets credit for the whole journey.

It doesn’t show which one they used first, how often they searched, what they searched for or whether they bought anything. It also doesn’t capture the full use of either service through apps.

#5506. Billionaire Brian Chesky’s social-worker parents told him to pick a high-paying career. He went to art school—and started Airbnb with 3 air beds

Before Airbnb had over 9 million listings worldwide, there was one sole lodging: three inflatable air beds at CEO Brian Chesky’s San Francisco home. He had quit his job and packed up all his belongings in a Honda Civic to make a cross-country move, and couldn’t pay his rent. That’s when he noticed all the local hotels were booked because of the Industrial Designers Society of America’s International Design Conference in San Francisco, and a business was born.

“We called it the air-bed-and-breakfast,” he told Fortune in 2017 at a World’s Greatest Leaders event.

Chesky and Airbnb cofounder Joe Gebbia were hooked on the idea of making money and meeting new friends through their makeshift accommodations, so they opened their home to three guests: “What if you could book someone’s home the way you could book a hotel anywhere in the world?” Chesky said about their inspiration. They launched Airbnb with Gebbia’s former roommate Nathan Blecharczyk in 2008.

Chesky’s social-worker parents in upstate New York (he was born in Albany) told him to pursue a high-paying career, but much to their chagrin he went to art school instead, at the famous Rhode Island School of Design.

“I’m going to become an artist,” Chesky recalls telling his mom, to which she responded: “You somehow managed to pick the only job in the world that pays less than a social worker. You’ll get paid nothing.”

Today, Chesky doesn’t have to worry as much.

Airbnb has a market capitalization of $112 billion, above its level from before the pandemic, which threatened its very survival as a business. The company lost 80% of its business in the first months of the pandemic, and Chesky reorganized it in a scramble for survival.

Though Chesky’s creativity is what birthed (and saved) Airbnb, it also meant business veterans did not initially take him seriously.

Chesky’s design background was at first a hindrance to a budding Airbnb. While looking for $150,000 to fund an estimated 10% of the company, Chesky met with over 20 potential investors, all of whom turned him down.

“Joe and I were designers, and as far as they were concerned, designers didn’t start companies,” Chesky said. “We didn’t look like a tech founder, which is ridiculous because I don’t think you should ever hire somebody because they look like something else. You want a new thing.”

Investors didn’t take an interest in Airbnb until it began designing presidential-candidate-themed cereal boxes, which eventually got the attention of Paul Graham, founder of startup accelerator Y Combinator.

“Creative companies are companies that tap into a sense of imagination,” Chesky told Time. “That they might come up with new breakthrough ideas, that people that were only beholden to near-term measurable outcomes won’t ever have.”

Success at Airbnb has been a double-edged sword. Explosive growth has forced the company to refocus at times.

During the pandemic, Chesky told Fortune in 2023, he even opened his own home as an Airbnb to better understand the host experience and lived in various Airbnbs across the country for six months, where he discovered inconsistent and unnecessary practices across hosts, including complicated rent agreements.

Airbnb still faces challenges as waves of short-term rental regulations in New York and across Europe, where cities are implementing phase-outs, prohibiting rentals for less than 30 days, or no longer renewing tourist apartment licenses, for example. In the U.S., housing advocates have fought against Airbnb, according to the AP, claiming short-term rentals have essentially become hotels.

Airbnb has pushed back against regulations, saying that short-term rental bans would limit affordable accommodations for travelers.

Last month, Airbnb implemented a new “reasonable house rules and requests” policy, where the company has stopped asking guests to “complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner,” such as stripping the bed, washing and putting away dishes, or taking trash offsite. The new policy, which will go into effect on rentals booked on or after Nov. 20, has drawn pushback as hosts threaten to boycott or hike cleaning fees, and been a pleasant surprise to customers.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 24, 2024.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.
